spark.summary: An API gateway terminates external Layer 7 traffic (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSockets) at the edge, centralizing TLS termination, rate limiting, auth verification, and protocol translation before routing to internal services.
spark.keyTakeaway: Centralize cross-cutting edge concerns in a single L7 proxy, but keep business logic out of it so the gateway never becomes a monolithic bottleneck.

concept.whyItMatters: Without an L7 gateway, every microservice re-implements JWT validation, CORS, TLS 1.3 termination, and token-bucket rate limiting—often inconsistently. A dedicated proxy like Envoy or Kong handles 50k+ RPS per node at sub-millisecond p99 overhead while translating external REST/JSON or WebSockets into internal HTTP/2 gRPC streams.
whenToUse: Exposing dozens of internal gRPC or REST microservices under a unified public domain with consistent auth, rate limiting, and observability.
Supporting heterogeneous client protocols—such as browser HTTP/1.1 REST, mobile HTTP/2, and persistent RFC 6455 WebSocket connections—on one ingress tier.
Enforcing per-tenant quotas, canary traffic splitting (e.g., 95/5 weighted routing), and circuit breaking before requests hit backend compute.
whenNotToUse: Service-to-service east-west communication inside a trusted Kubernetes cluster where a sidecar service mesh (Istio/Cilium) or direct gRPC load balancing is cleaner.
Single-service monoliths or early-stage apps where a simple L4/L7 cloud load balancer (AWS ALB/NLB) already covers TLS and health checks.
Ultra-low-latency trading or HFT pipelines where an extra L7 proxy hop adds an unacceptable 300–800 µs serialization and buffering penalty.
keyPoints: Protocol termination and multiplexing: terminate external HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/3 (QUIC) at the edge and reuse long-lived HTTP/2 connections upstream to eliminate TCP/TLS handshake overhead.

REST vs. RPC vs. WebSockets: REST maps resources to HTTP verbs with JSON payloads; gRPC uses HTTP/2 binary frames and Protobuf for ~5–10x smaller payloads; WebSockets upgrade an HTTP/1.1 connection via 101 Switching Protocols for full-duplex streaming.

gRPC-Web and JSON transcoding: gateways like Envoy transcode external REST/JSON requests into internal gRPC calls using `.proto` descriptors so browsers can consume gRPC backends without custom clients.
Connection statefulness differs sharply: stateless REST requests can be load-balanced per request, whereas WebSockets pin a persistent TCP socket to a specific gateway worker for minutes or hours.

Backpressure and timeouts: independent upstream connect timeouts (e.g., 1s), request timeouts (e.g., 15s), and WebSocket idle timeouts prevent slowloris or hung backends from exhausting file descriptors.

examples.title: REST-to-gRPC Transcoding at an E-Commerce Edge
examples.scenario: A web storefront sends `POST /v1/orders` with a JSON body over HTTP/2, while the internal Order Service only speaks gRPC with Protobuf.
examples.outcome: Envoy's `grpc_json_transcoder` filter maps the REST path and JSON fields to `OrderService.CreateOrder`, cutting backend payload size by 72% and avoiding a separate BFF service.

examples.title: Isolating Stateful WebSocket Pools from Stateless REST
examples.scenario: A live sports dashboard maintains 400k concurrent WebSocket connections for score pushes alongside 30k RPS of stateless REST API reads.
examples.outcome: Splitting `/ws/*` onto a dedicated gateway fleet tuned with `ulimit -n 1048576` and 60s ping/pong heartbeats prevents long-lived socket memory pressure from starving short-lived REST worker threads.

tradeOffs.pro: One Envoy/Kong fleet keeps TLS, WAF, and rate-limiting policies in a single declarative config.
tradeOffs.con: Aggregating 5+ downstream calls inside gateway Lua/Wasm plugins couples teams to the edge tier and slows deployments.

tradeOffs.factor: gRPC vs. REST/JSON at the Public Edge
tradeOffs.pro: HTTP/2 multiplexing and Protobuf schemas give strict contracts, streaming, and lower bandwidth.
tradeOffs.con: Browser clients require gRPC-Web proxies, and payloads are opaque in standard curl/browser DevTools.

tradeOffs.factor: Centralized Rate Limiting vs. Local Token Buckets
tradeOffs.pro: Redis-backed global counters enforce exact per-tenant limits across 20+ gateway pods.
tradeOffs.con: Every request incurs a 1–2 ms Redis round-trip unless local burst caching or asynchronous sync is used.

failureModes.name: WebSocket File Descriptor Exhaustion
failureModes.description: Each concurrent WebSocket holds an open downstream and upstream socket; a surge of 100k reconnects after a deploy hits the OS `nofile` limit or ephemeral port ceiling (65,535).
failureModes.mitigation: Raise `fs.file-max` and `ulimit -n`, bind multiple local IP aliases for upstream NAT ports, and enforce jittered exponential backoff in client reconnect logic.

failureModes.name: Cascading Retries (Retry Storm)
failureModes.description: Gateway auto-retries on `502`/`504` multiply load 3x–5x against an already degraded upstream service, turning a brief GC pause into a total outage.
failureModes.mitigation: Cap retries to idempotent methods (`GET`/`HEAD`) with a strict retry budget (e.g., max 20% of active requests) and per-try timeouts.

failureModes.name: Head-of-Line Blocking on HTTP/1.1 Upstream Pools
failureModes.description: Misconfigured HTTP/1.1 upstream pools without pipelining or sufficient max connections stall queued requests behind slow responses.
failureModes.mitigation: Upgrade upstream pools to HTTP/2 multiplexing (`h2c` or TLS) and size `max_connections` and `max_pending_requests` with circuit breakers.

failureModes.name: Plugin Memory Leak in Lua/Wasm Filters
failureModes.description: Custom body-buffering plugins that read multi-megabyte payloads into memory cause OOMKills across gateway pods under high concurrency.
failureModes.mitigation: Stream request/response bodies without full buffering whenever possible and enforce strict `max_request_bytes` limits (e.g., 4 MB) at the listener.

commonMistakes: Embedding domain orchestration and database lookups directly inside gateway plugins, turning the proxy into a single point of failure.
Applying the same 10-second HTTP request timeout to WebSocket or Server-Sent Events (SSE) routes, silently killing live streams.
Forgetting to strip or overwrite untrusted `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Real-IP` headers at the outermost edge, enabling IP-spoofed rate-limit bypasses.
Sharing one global connection pool across fast health checks and slow file-upload endpoints, causing thread/connection starvation.
Ignoring HTTP/2 `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` limits (often defaulting to 100), which bottlenecks high-throughput gRPC over a single upstream TCP connection.

sections.content:
## The idea

An API gateway is a reverse proxy operating at OSI Layer 7 (Application Layer). Unlike a Layer 4 load balancer that forwards raw TCP/UDP packets based only on IP and port, an L7 gateway parses HTTP headers, paths, cookies, gRPC metadata, and WebSocket upgrade handshakes. Because it understands the request envelope, it can authenticate JWTs, enforce per-route rate limits, translate REST/JSON to internal gRPC/Protobuf, and route `/ws` traffic to stateful socket backends—all before a single byte reaches application code.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider a client calling `POST https://api.acme.io/v2/payments` over HTTP/2 while a second tab opens `wss://api.acme.io/ws/ticker`.

1. **TLS & L7 Parse**: Envoy terminates TLS 1.3 (ALPN `h2` for the API call, `http/1.1` for the WebSocket upgrade). It normalizes headers and sets `X-Request-ID`.
2. **Filter Chain**: For `/v2/payments`, Envoy validates the `Authorization: Bearer` JWT signature locally against a cached JWKS, checks a token-bucket rate limiter (e.g., 500 req/min per `sub`), and runs `grpc_json_transcoder` to serialize the JSON body into a Protobuf frame.
3. **Upstream Dispatch**: Envoy selects a healthy endpoint from its `payments-grpc` cluster over a pre-warmed HTTP/2 connection pool and forwards the `HEADERS` + `DATA` frames.
4. **WebSocket Upgrade**: For `/ws/ticker`, Envoy sees `Connection: Upgrade` and `Upgrade: websocket`, bypasses JSON transcoding, establishes a dedicated bidirectional tunnel to `ticker-ws` pod `:8080`, and relays `101 Switching Protocols` back to the browser.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / REST, RPC, and WebSockets under the hood
sections.content:
## REST, RPC, and WebSockets under the hood

Each Layer 7 protocol optimizes for a different interaction pattern and imposes distinct demands on the gateway:

- **REST (HTTP/1.1 & HTTP/2)**: Resource-oriented, text-based (JSON), cacheable via `ETag`/`Cache-Control`. Easy to inspect and debug, but verbose headers and JSON parsing burn CPU at high RPS.
- **gRPC (HTTP/2 + Protobuf)**: Contract-first binary RPC supporting unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, and bidirectional streams. Requires HTTP/2 framing (`DATA` + trailing `HEADERS` for `grpc-status`), so L4 proxies cannot load-balance individual RPCs—only L7 gateways can.
- **WebSockets (RFC 6455)**: Starts as an HTTP/1.1 `GET` with `Upgrade: websocket`, then drops HTTP framing entirely in favor of lightweight 2–14 byte binary/text frames over the same TCP socket. Because the connection is stateful, rolling restarts on the gateway require graceful connection draining (`GOAWAY` or staggered close frames) to avoid thundering-herd reconnects.

## Protocol comparison for gateway routing

| Dimension | REST (HTTP/1.1 & HTTP/2) | gRPC (HTTP/2 + Protobuf) | WebSockets (RFC 6455) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Connection Model** | Stateless request/response | Multiplexed streams over long-lived TCP | Persistent full-duplex TCP tunnel |
| **Payload Format** | JSON / UTF-8 text | Binary Protobuf (schema-enforced) | Arbitrary text or binary frames |
| **Load Balancing** | Per-request L7 round-robin | Per-RPC L7 stream balancing | Per-connection (sticky for socket life) |
| **Browser Support** | Native `fetch()` | Needs `grpc-web` proxy/transcoding | Native `new WebSocket()` |
| **Gateway Overhead** | Medium (JSON + header parsing) | Low (binary framing, HPACK) | Low per frame; high open-FD memory |
| **Primary Timeout** | Request timeout (e.g., 5–30s) | Per-RPC deadline (`grpc-timeout`) | Idle / heartbeat ping timeout (e.g., 60s) |

## Failure modes

1. **gRPC Connection Pinning**: Placing a Layer 4 NLB in front of gRPC backends without L7 awareness pins all multiplexed streams from one client onto a single backend pod. Fix: terminate and re-originate HTTP/2 at an L7 gateway (Envoy/Linkerd).
2. **Thundering Herd on WebSocket Deploy**: Restarting 20 gateway pods simultaneously drops 500k sockets, causing clients to reconnect at the exact same millisecond and overwhelm TLS handshakes. Fix: drain connections gradually over 5–10 minutes with jittered client backoff.
3. **Buffer Bloat on Large Payloads**: Gateways buffering 50 MB file uploads in RAM before forwarding cause tail-latency spikes and OOMKills. Fix: stream bodies directly or route uploads via pre-signed S3/GCS URLs.
4. **Header Spoofing**: Trusting client-supplied `X-Forwarded-For` or `X-User-Id` lets attackers bypass IP allowlists or impersonate users. Fix: strip internal trust headers at the edge and overwrite them only after verified auth.

## Choosing your gateway topology

Small-to-midsize platforms do best with a single managed or ingress-integrated L7 gateway (Kong, Envoy Gateway, or AWS API Gateway) handling TLS, JWT verification, and routing. Once WebSocket or streaming volume exceeds ~50k concurrent connections, split stateful `/ws` listeners onto a dedicated autoscaling pool so memory-heavy long-lived sockets never compete with latency-sensitive REST/gRPC traffic. Keep business aggregation in a separate BFF service behind the gateway.

## Practical checklist

- **Separate timeouts by route**: set strict 5–15s request timeouts on REST/gRPC routes and explicit 60s idle + ping/pong timeouts on WebSocket routes.
- **Enforce HTTP/2 upstream pools**: configure `h2` or `h2c` between gateway and backends and raise `max_concurrent_streams` above 100 for high-RPS gRPC.
- **Cap retry budgets**: allow automatic retries only on idempotent `GET`/`HEAD` requests, bounded to <=20% of active traffic, with per-try timeouts.
- **Sanitize edge headers**: strip `X-User-*` and untrusted `X-Forwarded-For` hops at the outermost listener before any auth filter runs.
- **Monitor L7 saturation metrics**: alert on `upstream_rq_pending_overflow`, `downstream_cx_active` vs. `ulimit -n`, and `502`/`504` ratios per route.

dimensions.description: Applying API Gateway & Layer 7 Protocols: REST, RPC, WebSockets effectively.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Deploy API Gateway & Layer 7 Protocols: REST, RPC, WebSockets with strict monitoring thresholds and graceful degradation fallbacks.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: An API gateway terminates external Layer 7 traffic (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSockets) at the edge, centralizing TLS termination, rate limiting, auth verification, and protocol translation before routing to internal services.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Payments Service applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Ticker Streamer.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Ticker Streamer experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Raise `fs.file-max` and `ulimit -n`, bind multiple local IP aliases for upstream NAT ports, and enforce jittered exponential backoff in client reconnect logic.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Centralize cross-cutting edge concerns in a single L7 proxy, but keep business logic out of it so the gateway never becomes a monolithic bottleneck.
Avoid trap: Embedding domain orchestration and database lookups directly inside gateway plugins, turning the proxy into a single point of failure.
Avoid trap: Applying the same 10-second HTTP request timeout to WebSocket or Server-Sent Events (SSE) routes, silently killing live streams.
When to reach for it: Exposing dozens of internal gRPC or REST microservices under a unified public domain with consistent auth, rate limiting, and observability.
When to reach for it: Supporting heterogeneous client protocols—such as browser HTTP/1.1 REST, mobile HTTP/2, and persistent RFC 6455 WebSocket connections—on one ingress tier.

putItTogether.title: Putting Api Gateway Together
putItTogether.summary: Centralize cross-cutting edge concerns in a single L7 proxy, but keep business logic out of it so the gateway never becomes a monolithic bottleneck.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Api Gateway before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Envoy's `grpc_json_transcoder` filter maps the REST path and JSON fields to `OrderService.CreateOrder`, cutting backend payload size by 72% and avoiding a separate BFF service.
